deep.reconstruction:
PART 1 (continuation of the 20 April experiments on the previous page). On the previous page Gauss tabulated, for 12 circle positions x = 15°, 45°, ..., 345°, microscope readings a and b. He derived a periodic term f(x) and fitted it by f(x) ≈ −0.75'' cos x + 0.36'' sin x, which is the standard first-harmonic (eccentricity-type) correction. He then gave a mean reading error of sqrt(0.68625) = 0.828''. Here he writes: "to represent the above experiments with this, one must assume the following reading errors". There follow 36 residuals v_ij, i = 1..12 (one row per position) and j = 1..3 (columns). A check (mine) shows that every row sums to zero within ±0.01: e.g. +0.21 − 0.58 + 0.38 = 0.01 and −1.43 + 0.72 + 0.71 = 0. So within each position the three columns are residuals of three related readings, constrained to sum to zero, i.e. an adjustment within each row. The column sums are small: +0.06, +0.12, −0.14. The total sum of squares is Σv² ≈ 10.07. The page does not state exactly how these 36 values were obtained from the previous page's a, b and f(x); I do not claim a precise derivation beyond the zero-row-sum structure.

PART 2 (22 April): determining the scale value of the axis level (Axenlibelle). The level was hung on the balance bar (Balancirstange), which was tilted by known amounts read on the microscope as 89°45' + t, with t = 2'0'', 2'25'', 2'50'', 3'0'', 3'5'', 3'10''. For each tilt the right and left bubble-end readings R and L (in partes) were recorded. With the trial value 1'' = 0.4 p, each reading is reduced to the common setting t0 = 2'40'': R' = R − 0.4(t0 − t) and L' = L + 0.4(t0 − t). Examples:
- t = 2'0'': Δ = 40'' = 16 p, so R' = 34.6 − 16 = 18.6 and L' = 2.6 + 16 = 18.6.
- t = 2'25'': R' = 24.3 − 6 = 18.3 and L' = 13.1 + 6 = 19.1.
- t = 2'50'': R' = 13.6 + 4 = 17.6 and L' = 23.8 − 4 = 19.8.
- t = 3'0'': R' = 11.0 + 8 = 19.0 and L' = 27.0 − 8 = 19.0.
- t = 3'5'': R' = 9.1 + 10 = 19.1 and L' = 28.6 − 10 = 18.6.
- t = 3'10'': R' = 6.5 + 12 = 18.5 and L' = 31.2 − 12 = 19.2. Gauss wrote 19.1.
The reduced values are constant to within about ±1 p, which confirms the scale value. My own least-squares check over the 70'' range gives slopes of −0.396 p/'' for the right end and +0.405 p/'' for the left end, mean ≈ 0.400 p/''. The bubble length R + L grows slightly, from 37.2 to 38.0, presumably a temperature effect.

The conclusions are: 1 pars = 2.5'' = 1.74 mm (the mm value of one division is taken as known); 1 mm = 1/1.74 p = 0.575 p = 1.44''; 1'' = 0.4 p = 0.696 mm. Implied (my addition): the radius of curvature of the level vial is ≈ 206265/1.437 mm ≈ 143.5 m.
errors: Reduction of the last row (3'10''): 31.2 − 12 = 19.2, but 19.1 is written. This is a 0.1 p slip, unless the left reading is 31.1.
No real errors in the unit conversions: 1/1.74 = 0.5747 ≈ 0.575 p; 2.5/1.74 = 1.437 ≈ 1.44''; 0.4 × 1.74 = 0.696 mm. All are consistent.

The relation between the 36 tabulated residuals and the mean error 0.828'' on the previous page is not explicit. Σv²/36 ≈ 0.28 does not equal 0.686, so a different divisor or definition is involved and cannot be checked from this page alone.

results.what: Assignment of individual reading residuals (36 values, three per position, each triple summing to zero) consistent with a fitted first-harmonic correction −0.75 cos x + 0.36 sin x of a divided circle
results.modern_name: Residual analysis in least-squares adjustment of graduation/eccentricity errors
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss/Bessel (least squares; circle-division error studies, early 19th c.)

results.what: Calibration of a spirit level's scale value by tilting it on a balance bar through measured small angles and reducing bubble readings to a common setting; 1'' = 0.4 partes = 0.696 mm
results.modern_name: Level-tester (Libellenprüfer) determination of a spirit level's sensitivity / scale value
results.usually_credited_to: Standard astronomical-geodetic practice (Reichenbach, Bessel, Gauss era)

deep.surprise_reason: This is routine observational instrument calibration: residuals of a harmonic fit and the scale value of an axis level. It is typical of Gauss's documented geodetic and astronomical practice and contains no new mathematics.

checkable.asserts: Right-end readings reduced to 2'40'' with 0.4 p/'' give 18.6, 18.3, 17.6, 19.0, 19.1, 18.5
Left-end reduced values are 18.6, 19.1, 19.8, 19.0, 18.6, 19.2 (the manuscript has 19.1 for the last)
Least-squares slope of the right bubble end is ≈ −0.396 partes per arcsecond, i.e. scale ≈ 0.4 p/''
Each residual triple sums to 0 within ±0.01; total sum of squares ≈ 10.07
Implied radius of curvature of the axis level vial ≈ 143.5 m

transcription_corrections: Line 'Um dein Scalenwerth' should read 'Um den Scalenwerth' (the word is overwritten in the manuscript).
In the last residual row the middle entry is overwritten; −0,51 is the most plausible reading and is consistent with the row summing to zero (0.75 − 0.51 − 0.23 = 0.01).
The header reads '1'' = 0,4 partes', with 'partes' written above the 0,4; a small 'p' is written above the first right reading 34,6.
The columns '18,6 18,6 ...' are the reduced right and left readings under the heading 'Reducirt mit 1''=0p,4 auf 2'40''', and 'Apr 22' is a marginal date.
